notes.definition: Our solar system contains one star, the Sun, with eight planets and the dwarf planets that orbit it, and natural satellites (moons) that orbit the planets. It is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy and formed from a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity.
explanation: Within our solar system there is one star, the Sun. Eight planets orbit the Sun: in order from the Sun, Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The four inner planets are small and rocky; the four outer planets are much larger gas giants and ice giants. Dwarf planets, such as Pluto, also orbit the Sun but are much smaller than planets.

Natural satellites, the moons that orbit planets, are also part of the solar system. The Earth has one moon; Jupiter and Saturn each have dozens. Our solar system is only a small part of the Milky Way galaxy, which contains billions of stars. The Milky Way itself is just one of billions of galaxies in the universe.

The Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas called a nebula. Gravitational attraction pulled the dust and gas together. As the material fell inwards, it got denser and hotter, forming a protostar. Eventually the temperature and pressure at the centre became high enough for hydrogen nuclei to fuse together to form helium nuclei. These nuclear fusion reactions release enormous amounts of energy, and the star began to shine.

Once fusion starts, the energy released heats the core and produces an outward pressure (an expansion force). Gravity pulls the material of the star inwards (gravitational collapse). When these two are balanced, the star is in equilibrium and stays a stable size for a very long time. This is the main sequence stage of a star's life, which the Sun has been in for about 4.6 billion years and will stay in for billions more.
keyFacts: Our solar system has one star: the Sun.
Eight planets orbit the Sun; dwarf planets such as Pluto also orbit it.
Planet order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Natural satellites (moons) orbit planets and are part of the solar system.
The solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.
The Sun formed from a cloud of dust and gas (a nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.
Gravity made the core hot and dense enough for nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.
In a stable star, inward gravity is balanced by outward pressure from fusion energy: equilibrium.

keyTerms.definition: The Sun and everything that orbits it, including planets, dwarf planets and their moons.
A large body that orbits a star; there are eight in our solar system.
A body that orbits the Sun but is much smaller than a planet, such as Pluto.
A natural body, such as a moon, that orbits a planet.
A huge collection of billions of stars held together by gravity; ours is the Milky Way.
A cloud of dust and gas in space from which stars form.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.

workedExamples.title: Classifying objects
workedExamples.question: Classify each of these: the Moon, Pluto, the Sun, Mars, the Milky Way.
steps: The Moon orbits the Earth: a natural satellite.
Pluto orbits the Sun but is small: a dwarf planet.
The Sun is the star at the centre of the solar system.
Mars orbits the Sun: a planet.
The Milky Way is the galaxy that contains our solar system.
workedExamples.answer: Moon: natural satellite; Pluto: dwarf planet; Sun: star; Mars: planet; Milky Way: galaxy.

workedExamples.title: Why the Sun does not collapse
workedExamples.question: Explain why the Sun stays the same size even though gravity pulls its material inwards.
steps: Gravity acts inwards on all of the Sun's material.
Fusion in the core releases energy, creating an outward pressure.
These are balanced, so the Sun is in equilibrium.
workedExamples.answer: The inward pull of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure due to fusion energy.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the solar system and the galaxy are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact the solar system is one star and its orbiting bodies; the Milky Way galaxy contains billions of stars, and our solar system is a tiny part of it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the Sun is burning like a fire.
misconceptions.right: In fact the Sun releases energy by nuclear fusion of hydrogen nuclei into helium, not by chemical burning.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the Moon orbits the Sun directly like a planet.
misconceptions.right: In fact the Moon is a natural satellite that orbits the Earth (and moves round the Sun with the Earth).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a star stops collapsing because gravity switches off.
misconceptions.right: In fact gravity always acts; the star is stable because outward pressure from fusion energy balances it.

realWorld: Space probes such as Voyager, Juno and Cassini have visited planets and moons to study them close up.
Astronomers search for planets around other stars (exoplanets), many found by the dimming of the star as a planet passes in front.
Fusion reactors being developed on Earth try to copy the energy release that powers the Sun.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Physics (8463) only, not Combined Science.

Explain how, at the start of a star's life, dust and gas drawn together by gravity cause fusion reactions, and how fusion leads to an equilibrium between gravitational collapse and expansion due to fusion energy.
examTips: Learn the planet order with a mnemonic such as 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming'.
Use 'nebula', 'gravitational attraction', 'fusion' and 'equilibrium' when describing how the Sun formed.
When explaining stability, name both forces: gravity inwards and outward pressure (expansion) due to fusion energy.
Do not mix up moon (orbits a planet), planet (orbits a star) and galaxy (billions of stars).
summary: One star, eight planets, dwarf planets and moons make up the solar system.
The solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.
The Sun formed from a nebula pulled together by gravity.
Fusion began when the core became hot and dense enough.
Gravity and fusion pressure balance in a stable star.

questions.question: How many stars are there in our solar system?
markScheme: 1 mark: One
questions.explanation: The Sun is the only star in our solar system. Billions of stars are in the Milky Way galaxy.

questions.question: Which object is a natural satellite?
markScheme: 1 mark: The Moon
questions.explanation: The Moon orbits the Earth, so it is a natural satellite. Mars is a planet; the Sun is a star.

questions.question: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our solar system?
markScheme: 1 mark: The Milky Way
questions.explanation: Our solar system is part of the Milky Way galaxy. Andromeda is a different galaxy.

questions.question: Which of these is a dwarf planet?
markScheme: 1 mark: Pluto
questions.explanation: Pluto is a dwarf planet. Jupiter and Venus are planets; the Moon is a natural satellite.

questions.question: What did the Sun form from?
options: A cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity
markScheme: 1 mark: A cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity
questions.explanation: The Sun formed from a nebula, a cloud of dust and gas, pulled together by gravitational attraction.

questions.question: Which process releases energy in the core of the Sun?
options: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
markScheme: 1 mark: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium
questions.explanation: Hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium nuclei, releasing energy. It is not a chemical reaction.

questions.question: What is the correct order of size, from smallest to largest?
markScheme: 1 mark: Planet, solar system, galaxy
questions.explanation: A planet is part of a solar system, which is a small part of a galaxy.

questions.question: Which planet is fourth from the Sun?
markScheme: 1 mark: Mars
questions.explanation: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, so Mars is fourth.

questions.question: Why does a main sequence star such as the Sun stay a stable size for billions of years?
options: Gravity is zero inside a star
The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from fusion energy
markScheme: 1 mark: The inward force of gravity is balanced by the outward pressure from fusion energy
questions.explanation: Equilibrium between gravitational collapse and expansion due to fusion energy keeps the star stable.

questions.question: Why did fusion begin in the protostar that became the Sun?
options: Gravity made the core hot and dense enough for nuclei to fuse
The core cooled until nuclei stuck together
markScheme: 1 mark: Gravity made the core hot and dense enough for nuclei to fuse
questions.explanation: As gravity pulled material inwards, the core temperature and density rose until nuclei collided with enough energy to fuse.

questions.question: Name two types of object, other than the Sun, that are part of our solar system.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: planets; dwarf planets; moons (natural satellites)
questions.explanation: The solar system includes everything orbiting the Sun and the moons orbiting planets.

questions.question: State what is meant by a natural satellite.
markScheme: 1 mark: a natural object (such as a moon) that orbits a planet
questions.explanation: Natural satellites are not made by humans; artificial satellites are.

questions.question: State the name given to a cloud of dust and gas in space from which stars form.
markScheme: 1 mark: nebula
questions.explanation: Stars, including the Sun, form from nebulae.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a planet and a moon.
markScheme: 1 mark: a planet orbits a star (the Sun)
1 mark: a moon orbits a planet
questions.explanation: Both are held in orbit by gravity, but they orbit different types of object.

questions.question: Explain the role of gravity in the formation of the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravitational attraction pulled the dust and gas of the nebula together
1 mark: the material became denser and hotter until fusion could start
questions.explanation: Gravity drives the collapse that heats the core enough for fusion.

questions.question: Describe where our solar system is in the universe.
markScheme: 1 mark: it is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
1 mark: the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies in the universe
questions.explanation: This shows the scale: solar system, galaxy, universe.

questions.question: Explain how fusion reactions keep a star such as the Sun in equilibrium.
markScheme: 1 mark: fusion releases energy that heats the core
1 mark: this creates an outward pressure (expansion force)
1 mark: which balances the inward pull of gravity, so the star is stable
questions.explanation: Equilibrium means the inward and outward effects are equal, so the star neither collapses nor expands.

questions.question: Suggest what would happen to a star if the rate of fusion in its core suddenly decreased.
markScheme: 1 mark: the outward pressure would decrease, so gravity would be greater than the outward force
1 mark: the star would contract (shrink) until a new balance was reached
questions.explanation: When the forces are unbalanced, the star changes size until equilibrium is restored.

questions.question: Name the planets nearest to and furthest from the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: nearest: Mercury
1 mark: furthest: Neptune
questions.explanation: Pluto was once called the furthest planet but is now classed as a dwarf planet.

questions.question: Compare the four inner planets with the four outer planets.
markScheme: 1 mark: the inner planets (Mercury to Mars) are small and rocky
1 mark: the outer planets (Jupiter to Neptune) are much larger gas or ice giants
questions.explanation: This difference arose as the solar system formed from the nebula.

questions.question: Describe the structure of our solar system and its place in the universe.
markScheme: Indicative content: one star, the Sun, at the centre; eight planets orbit the Sun (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune); inner rocky, outer gas giants; dwarf planets such as Pluto orbit the Sun; natural satellites (moons) orbit planets; held in orbit by gravity; the solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy; the Milky Way is one of billions of galaxies.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear description of the main bodies and their relationships, and the position in the galaxy.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple list of bodies with little organisation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A good answer moves from the Sun outwards and then zooms out to the galaxy.

questions.question: Explain how the Sun formed and why it has remained a stable star for billions of years.
markScheme: Indicative content: the Sun formed from a nebula (cloud of dust and gas); gravitational attraction pulled the material together; as it collapsed it became denser and hotter (gravitational energy transferred to thermal store); a protostar formed; when the core was hot and dense enough, hydrogen nuclei fused to form helium; fusion releases large amounts of energy; star began to shine; energy from fusion produces outward pressure (expansion); gravity pulls inwards (collapse); forces balanced: equilibrium; star stable on the main sequence for billions of years while hydrogen fuel lasts.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, logically sequenced explanation of formation and of equilibrium, using correct terms.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): explains formation or equilibrium well, with some detail of the other.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, such as the Sun formed from gas and dust.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The two halves: gravity drives formation and fusion; fusion pressure then balances gravity.

questions.question: Which object orbits the Earth?
markScheme: 1 mark: The Moon
questions.explanation: The Moon is the Earth's natural satellite. The Earth orbits the Sun.

questions.question: Name the force that keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun.
markScheme: 1 mark: gravity (gravitational attraction)
questions.explanation: Gravity provides the force that keeps planets and moons in their orbits.

questions.question: Before fusion started, why did the protostar that formed the Sun get hotter?
options: As gravity pulled particles inwards, their speed increased and they collided more, raising the temperature
Light from other stars heated it
Radioactive decay of iron heated it
markScheme: 1 mark: As gravity pulled particles inwards, their speed increased and they collided more, raising the temperature
questions.explanation: Gravitational collapse transfers energy to the kinetic store of the particles, so the temperature rises until fusion can begin.

questions.question: Compare a planet, a dwarf planet and a natural satellite.
markScheme: Indicative content: planet: large body orbiting the Sun (eight in our solar system); dwarf planet: also orbits the Sun but much smaller, such as Pluto; natural satellite: orbits a planet, such as the Moon; all held in orbit by gravity; all are part of the solar system; all reflect light from the Sun rather than producing their own.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear comparison including what each orbits and at least one similarity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or two of the objects.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is size and what each body orbits.
